item.title: New Abuse of the ClickOnce Technology, Part 2: Stop Threat Actors from Clicking Once and Staying Forever
item.description:
ClickOnce weaponized for stealthy delivery, persistence, and COM hijacking. Attackers abuse Microsoft's own deployment tech to execute malware inside legitimate process trees without elevated privileges.
Key findings: - Payload runs under rundll32.exe and dfsvc.exe, legitimate Microsoft processes, giving threat actors built-in LOLBins cover. .application and .appref-ms files bypass mailbox filters and SmartScreen scrutiny that would catch a plain .exe. - The .appref-ms shortcut dropped to %Users\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\ is a persistence artifact. Place it in Startup or wire it to a scheduled task and the C2 payload silently updates every time it runs, no user prompt, no UAC, no admin rights required. - Trojanizing signed app dependencies (dependency hijacking or new deployment creation) lets attackers inherit a trusted signature without breaking it, sliding past SmartScreen entirely. - CrowdStrike identified what it believes is a new COM hijacking abuse surface discovered inside dfdll!BindToServer(), adding another vector to an already underdiscussed attack surface.
Hunt for .appref-ms files outside the Start Menu Programs path, scheduled tasks or Startup folder entries pointing to .appref-ms, and child processes of dfsvc.exe or rundll32.exe making outbound connections. Flag unsigned ClickOnce deployments and audit dependency manifests on any ClickOnce app in your environment.

item.title: Killing me gently: Inside Gentlemen’s EDR killer framework
item.description:
Gentlemen RaaS operates a centrally maintained EDR-killer suite, GentleKiller, with 8 BYOVD variants targeting 400+ processes across 48 security vendors, confirmed by a May 2026 internal data leak.
Key findings:
- GentleKiller is Gentlemen's in-house BYOVD framework (T1543.003), deploying vulnerable drivers including eb.sys (rootkit), stpm_old/new.sys (Safetica), dmx.sys (Zemana WatchDog), and PoisonX. Eight variants impersonate gaming and security software (FaceIT, Valorant, EA Anti-Cheat) and kill 400+ processes covering CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, ESET, Sophos, Microsoft Defender, Sysmon64.exe, and more. New BYOVD PoCs are operationalized within days of public release.
- The suite also integrates HexKiller (abusing googleApiUtil64.sys, Baidu BdApi driver), ThrottleBlood (ThrottleBlood.sys), and HavocKiller (havoc.sys, Huawei Audio driver), all re-wrapped with Gentlemen's shared evasion layer: Enigma/Themida packing, fake version info, copied invalid certificates, and vendor-impersonating filenames (T1036.001, T1027).
- OxideHarvest (buildx641.exe, SHA-1 A5CF917EC4A7DFBDFA43) is a Rust credential stealer tied to a Gentlemen affiliate, harvesting Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Brave profile data via multithreaded lateral credential spraying.
- Tools are staged consistently in a directory named GentlemenCollection across unrelated intrusions, giving responders a reliable filesystem artifact for attribution.

item.title: AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent
item.description:
AutoJack: a three-flaw chain in AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket lets a malicious webpage rendered by a local browsing agent spawn arbitrary processes on the developer's host with no user interaction beyond visiting a URL.
Key findings: - Three weaknesses chain together: Origin allowlist bypassed because the agent's headless browser is localhost (CWE-1385), auth middleware explicitly skipping /api/mcp/* with no handler picking up the check (CWE-306), and server_params decoded from the URL passed verbatim to stdio_client as a command line (CWE-78), accepting calc.exe, powershell.exe, or bash as valid "MCP servers" - Attack flow: attacker page serves JavaScript that opens ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/?server_params= with a base64 payload, agent's MultimodalWebSurfer renders it, AutoGen Studio spawns the command under the developer's account, no token required regardless of auth mode configured - Affected code never shipped in a PyPI release; exposure limited to developers who built from the main GitHub branch before hardening commit b047730, which adds server-side parameter binding via a POST/UUID flow and removes /api/mcp from the auth skip list - Broader pattern: any agent that browses untrusted content and shares a host with a privileged local control plane dissolves the loopback trust boundary, this is not specific to AutoGen.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2067805271007559718

item.title: DCOM Explained: How Attackers Turn a Windows Feature into a Lateral Movement Tool
item.description:
DCOM lateral movement exploits native Windows RPC infrastructure to execute commands remotely without dropping a single malicious file, making process-chain correlation your primary detection lever.
Key findings: - Attack chain (T1021.003): attacker dumps creds from lsass.exe on Machine A, authenticates to Machine B over TCP 135, instantiates MMC20.Application via CLSID C085698C-D16F-417A-8851-A263C70D21B6, then calls ExecuteShellCommand. No payload dropped; only signed Windows binaries touch disk. - Four-event correlation catches it: Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 (NTLM network logon) + Sysmon Event ID 3 (TCP 135 connection between workstations) + Sysmon Event ID 1 showing mmc.exe or excel.exe spawned under svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch + cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a child of that DCOM host process. - The RPCSS Endpoint Mapper (rpcss.dll) handles port 135 negotiation and permission checks via HKCR\CLSID before SCM spawns the target process, so registry auditing on that key can surface unauthorized CLSID lookups. - Prevention: block TCP 135 between workstations at the firewall, strip remote activation rights from non-admin accounts in DCOM config, and deploy LAPS to break lateral reuse of local admin credentials.
Hunt for powershell.exe or cmd.exe whose grandparent is svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch. That two-hop parent chain is rare in legitimate traffic and is the clearest signal this technique leaves behind.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2067790451894333892

item.title: PeopleSoft PeopleTools Pre-Authentication RCE: A PSIGW SSRF Chain That Executes Inside the JVM
item.description:
Oracle PeopleSoft PeopleTools pre-auth RCE chain abuses the PSIGW Integration Broker gateway to execute arbitrary code inside the application JVM, no credentials required.
Key findings: - The attack chains an SSRF through the PSIGW gateway endpoint to reach internal services not exposed externally, then pivots to RCE executing directly inside the JVM, bypassing network perimeter controls entirely - Because execution happens inside the JVM process rather than spawning a child process, host-based behavioral sensors that watch for unusual process trees will miss this without JVM-level instrumentation - Pre-authentication means no valid account is needed, making every internet-exposed PeopleSoft instance a target from first contact - Affected component is PeopleSoft PeopleTools Integration Broker (PSIGW); patch and network segmentation status of the gateway endpoint are the first triage questions for any responder
Hunt for anomalous outbound connections or internal lateral movement originating from the PeopleSoft application server process itself. Check web server access logs for unexpected or malformed requests to /PSIGW/ endpoints. If you have JVM-level logging or Java security manager events, prioritize those over OS process telemetry here since that is where execution lives.

item.title: Why Would an Adversary Collect 74,000 FortiGate
item.description:
A 74,000-record FortiGate access inventory, spanning 21,000+ organizations globally, reveals a structured credential-collection and validation operation with active distributed backend infrastructure, not a simple dump.
Key findings: - The dataset contained internet-facing FortiGate endpoints, admin usernames, FortiGuard accounts, org identifiers, and credential data across telecom, energy, manufacturing, healthcare, and financial sectors. Repeated credential patterns across unrelated orgs confirm systematic validation, not opportunistic scraping. - ThreatMon identified a distributed backend with at least six agents actively pulling tasks as late as June 2, 2026. Agent source IPs: 185[.]229[.]26[.]83, 213[.]169[.]49[.]142, 38[.]117[.]87[.]37, 198[.]53[.]64[.]194, 175[.]155[.]64[.]221, 211[.]72[.]37[.]226. - The architecture resembles a large-scale credential-cracking and validation pipeline. Infrastructure was active before public disclosure, meaning the dataset is a snapshot of an ongoing operation, not its start. - Victim prioritization toward critical infrastructure and distributed enterprise environments points to pre-positioning for initial access brokering, ransomware staging, or supply-chain targeting rather than immediate exploitation.
Hunt: Pull FortiGate VPN and admin auth logs and cross-reference against the six infrastructure IPs above. Flag repeated auth failures, unexpected admin account creation, and config changes post-successful login.

item.title: FortiBleed: You Can't Patch Your Way Out of This
item.description:
FortiBleed: ~50% of internet-facing FortiGate firewalls compromised in an industrialized credential campaign. Patching alone does not evict persistence already installed below the OS.
Key findings: - Scale is staggering: 73,932 FortiGate URLs across 194 countries hit, ~1.16 billion auth attempts validated against 320,000+ targets. Credential sources combined the 2021 CVE-2018-13379 (CVSS 9.8) leak with live infostealer logs, meaning 25-character random passwords fell because they were keylogged, not guessed. - Post-compromise, the firewall becomes a passive sniffer, harvesting VPN, LDAP, and RADIUS credentials in transit and feeding them back into the attack pool. A 45-GPU Hashtopolis cluster cracked offline SSL VPN hashes. CVE-2024-21762 (CVSS 9.6) drives the symlink persistence in /data/etc/ and /data/lib/, surviving reboots and firmware upgrades. - CVE-2026-25815 (CVSS 3.2, exploited in the wild) is the quiet killer: a shared default key decrypts LDAP credentials out of any stolen config. Low score, catastrophic real-world impact. - The SHA-256 old-password field persists after upgrade until an admin logs in post-patch. It does not appear in a normal admin view, only in a super_admin config export. A fully patched device can still carry a crackable credential hash.
Takeaway: Export config as super_admin and audit the old-password field. Hunt /data/etc/ and /data/lib/ for unexpected symlinks. Check your org against the Hudson Rock lookup.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2067729705542025640

item.title: Tor-Based Clipper Malware Targets Wallet Seed Phrases
item.description:
USB-spread clipper malware routes C2 through bundled Tor, swaps crypto wallet addresses in real time, and steals BIP39 seed phrases, tracked by Microsoft since February 2026.
Key findings: - Attack chain starts with a .lnk shortcut on a USB drive. The malware hides real documents, replaces them with malicious shortcuts of the same name, then schedules tasks to self-propagate to any newly inserted USB (T1091, T1053.005). - Clipboard is polled every 500ms for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, and Monero addresses, BIP39 12/24-word seed phrases, and Ethereum/Bitcoin WIF private keys. Detected addresses are swapped for attacker-controlled lookalikes before the victim pastes (T1115). - C2 hides entirely inside Tor using a bundled portable Tor client and a local SOCKS5 proxy on port 9050, resolving .onion domains with no exposed IP. Five screenshots are captured every ten seconds and exfiltrated over the same channel. - An EVAL instruction from C2 downloads JavaScript into a file named "cfile" and executes it via Windows Script Host, turning a clipper into a full backdoor (T1059.007). All components are PyArmor-obfuscated, PyInstaller-packaged, and decrypted only at runtime. - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detects this as Trojan:Win32/CryptoBandits.A.
Hunt for wscript.exe or cscript.exe spawning child processes, any process establishing connections to localhost:9050, and screen-capture commands in PowerShell.

item.title: Lost in relocation: analysis of a new loader distributing CASTLESTEALER
item.description:
New loader OXLOADER delivers CASTLESTEALER infostealer via malicious Google Ads, with low static detection rates. Shellcode staged through the Windows .reloc section and DonutLoader marks deliberate evasion engineering from a likely Russian-speaking actor.
Key findings: - Malvertising chain: victims searching for Node.js clicked a sponsored result to node-js[.]prentiva99[.]info, redirected through app[.]miloyannopoulos[.]com, then served a batch script from Storj (SHA-256: fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37) that launched OXLOADER with UAC bypass via -Verb RunAs (T1548.002) - OXLOADER uses control-flow flattening, opaque predicates, MBA obfuscation, and self-modifying XOR decryption stubs to defeat static analysis; shellcode is hidden in the .reloc section (legitimate toolchains never emit code there) then copied to a RWX .xtext section inside a renamed dui70.dll copy with .ocx extension - Anti-analysis checks require 3+ CPUs, 3+ GB RAM, display refresh rate above 20 Hz via WMI Win32_VideoController, and abort on CIS GEOIDs or Russian 🇷🇺 LANGID 0x419; emulation is defeated by calling WNetAddConnection2W with a malformed resource and reading LastErrorValue directly from the TEB - CASTLESTEALER C2: 89[.]124[.]95[.]161 and 89[.]124[.]115[.]82; OXLOADER hashes include 9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d and c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe.

item.title: SmartApeSG Launches Okendo Reviews Supply Chain Attack
item.description:
SmartApeSG compromised the Okendo Reviews widget used by 18,000+ brands, injecting staged JavaScript into e-commerce sites reaching millions of visitors and funneling them toward RAT and infostealer payloads via ClickFix lures.
Key findings: - Supply chain reach was massive: one affected U.S. 🇺🇸 retailer alone draws ~7 million monthly visits. The widget loads on high-traffic storefront and product pages, so the malicious JS executed silently in visitor browsers with no action required from site owners. - The injected script (JS.Injection.SmartApeSG) used localStorage timestamp checks to suppress repeat execution and User-Agent filtering to skip mobile devices, targeting desktop users primed for ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA and Windows Run-dialog lures. - Infrastructure was hidden via XOR-decoded string fragments reassembled at runtime, with a randomized 8-character token appended and a dynamic script tag injected to pull the next stage from hxxps://api[.]wigetticks[.]com/logout/private-response[.]php?8D1V4th3 and hxxps://api[.]wizzleticks[.]com/claims/scope-schema[.]php?4ManBBdA. - End payloads align with prior SmartApeSG campaigns: NetSupport RAT, Remcos RAT, StealC, and Sectop RAT delivered via PowerShell or HTA downloaders after social engineering.
Hunt your proxy and DNS logs for requests to wigetticks[.]com and wizzleticks[.]com, and inspect CSP and SRI logs for third-party script loads from okendo[.]io around May 14.

item.title: LATAM Infrastructure Hit by Fortinet and Ivanti Exploits
item.description:
Operation Escaneo exposed: a coordinated campaign hit Mexican 🇲🇽 government, financial, and critical infrastructure targets via chained Fortinet and Ivanti exploits, leaving 1.3M+ records and Active Directory maps stolen.
Key findings: - Initial access via CVE-2022-42475, CVE-2024-21762 (FortiOS SSL-VPN) and CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2025-0282 (Ivanti Connect Secure), with PoC code tuned to avoid crashing targets. Lateral movement extended to GhostCat, EternalBlue, Zerologon, and Log4Shell. - Custom recon engine "Kimera" auto-scanned and triaged victims, feeding directly into the exploitation stage. Neo-reGeorg webshells landed first, then Chisel reverse tunnels (3,708 sessions over 13 days) and a GRE tunnel through a compromised Cisco router moved traffic below host-based detection. - Exfil included 1.3M personal records, a 407MB Active Directory map, live-streamed SSL private keys, SAP service-account hashes, and browser-stored passwords. Attackers reached SAP and Oracle for command execution inside victim networks. - The group was exposed by an open staging directory, a self-inflicted OPSEC failure that let CloudSEK reconstruct the full toolkit.
Hunt for GRE tunnels terminating at external IPs, Chisel TCP-over-HTTP sessions, and unexpected process execution under SAP or Oracle service accounts. Patch the listed Fortinet and Ivanti CVEs first; those are confirmed active entry points here.

item.title: FortiBleed Exposes Admin Passwords for 75,000 Fortinet Firewalls
item.description:
FortiBleed: plaintext admin passwords for ~75,000 internet-facing Fortinet 🇷🇺-linked threat group exposes firewall configs spanning 194 countries, hitting critical infrastructure and government networks worldwide.
Key findings: - Config exports, not just credential scrapes, are circulating for 73,932 unique firewall URLs across 21,632 domains. Named organizations include Foxconn, Samsung, Siemens, PwC, and multiple government agencies. Because exports contain data only visible from the device itself, attackers had actual device access at some point, not just intercepted login traffic. - The threat group ran ~1.16 billion credential attempts against 320,777 FortiGate targets and ~2.1 billion against 163,650 MSSQL systems. SSL VPN auth hashes were cracked using a 45-GPU Hashtopolis cluster. A Turkish 🇹🇷 NATO defense contractor is listed among fully compromised targets with classified documents allegedly stolen. - The dataset is formatted as an initial-access sales catalog, including company industry, revenue, and employee count per entry. Credentials were verified as working at multiple organizations by Kevin Beaumont. - Many devices still store passwords as SHA-256 with salt despite Fortinet moving to PBKDF2 in early 2025 firmware, because the upgrade only activates after an admin logs in post-patch.

item.title: From package to postinstall payload: Inside the Mastra npm supply chain compromise
item.description:
npm supply chain attack hits 140+ Mastra packages via account takeover, injecting a typosquat dependency that executes a multi-stage implant during npm install across dev and CI/CD environments.
The ehindero npm maintainer account was compromised and used to poison 140+ @mastra scope packages on June 17, 2026. Every poisoned package injected easy-day-js@^1.11.21 as a dependency, a deliberate typosquat of dayjs (57M+ weekly downloads). SemVer resolution pulled 1.11.22, the weaponized version containing a postinstall hook. Execution happened at install time, meaning no import was required to trigger the payload.
- Attack chain: clean bait version easy-day-js@1.11.21 published June 16 07:05 UTC, weaponized 1.11.22 followed June 17 01:01 UTC, then 140+ Mastra packages poisoned by 01:20 UTC. The anomaly: mastra@1.13.0 was published via GitHub Actions OIDC; 1.13.1 was manually pushed from ehindero2016@tutamail[.]com, with no matching repo changes.
- The 4,572-byte setup.cjs dropper used a rotated 40-string Base64 array (seed 0x4c11d) to hide C2 addresses. It disabled TLS via NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0, dropped tracking markers at TMPDIR/.pkg_history and TMPDIR/.pkg_logs (XOR 0x80 encoded), fetched a ~41KB second-stage from hxxps://23[.]254[.]164[.]92:8000/update/49890878, then self-deleted via fs.rmSync(__filename).
- The second-stage is a persistent tasking implant, not a one-shot stealer.

item.title: Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control
item.description:
USB-spread crypto clipper active since Feb 2026 bundles a portable Tor client for anonymous C2, steals seed phrases and private keys, and replaces clipboard wallet addresses in real time.
Key findings: - Initial access via malicious .lnk files on USB drives (T1091). The worm hides legitimate documents, clones them as shortcuts, and drops two obfuscated JavaScript payloads into C:\Users\Public\Documents\[5-char folder]. Persistence via two scheduled tasks (T1053.005): one for USB spreading, one for the stealer. - The clipper launches ugate.exe (renamed Tor binary) in a hidden window, waits 60 seconds for bootstrap, then polls .onion C2 every ~500ms. EVAL responses execute arbitrary JScript at runtime, making this a full backdoor, not just a stealer. C2 comms route through localhost:9050 via curl with --socks5-hostname (T1090). - Clipboard theft targets BIP39 seed phrases, Ethereum/Bitcoin WIF private keys, and six address formats (BTC legacy, P2SH, taproot, Bech32, Tron, Monero), replacing them with attacker addresses. Five screenshots captured 10 seconds apart are exfiltrated via /recvf.php. - Defender AV detects as Trojan:Win32/CryptoBandits.A. Defanged C2 sample: cgky6bn6ux5wvlybtmm3z255igt52ljml2ngnc5qp3cnw5jlglamisad[.]onion. Full hash and IOC list in the Microsoft report.
Hunt with the Microsoft-provided KQL: DeviceProcessEvents filtering curl.exe with "--socks5-hostname" and "localhost:9050".
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2067397573519024163

item.title: Applying software engineering discipline to threat detection
item.description:
Treating detection rules as software artifacts eliminates the tribal-knowledge failures that let misconfigured SIEM rules fire 4,000 times overnight with no owner, no history, and no rollback path.
Key details: - Every detection rule belongs in Git with metadata: ATT&CK technique ID, data source, author, last reviewed date, and an explicit owner with an escalation path. Rules without ownership accumulate silently and become functionally dead while appearing active. - Sigma (YAML-based, vendor-neutral) compiles to Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL, Elastic EQL, Chronicle YARA-L, and more via sigma-cli/pySigma. The SigmaHQ repo gives you a maintained baseline to fork, not a blank page. Watch for field-name portability failures: a rule can compile cleanly and match nothing if target schema fields differ. - Every rule needs two test fixtures in CI: one malicious event it must match, one benign event it must not. Pull requests missing both should be rejected automatically, the same gate you apply to application code. - New rules enter shadow mode first (minimum 7 days, writes to a separate index, no analyst alert) before promotion. YARA-X adds a yr compile CI step for file/memory rules and clean JSON/YAML pipeline output.
Practitioner takeaway: start with five high-value rules, a Git repo, and a sigma-cli CI check that rejects PRs without test coverage.

item.description:

item.title: The dual-use dilemma: Rethinking detection for remote access tool abuse
item.description:
RMM abuse surged in 2025 as ransomware groups weaponized legitimate IT tools like ScreenConnect, NetSupport, and SimpleHelp, chaining multiple agents on single hosts to survive takedowns.
Key findings: - Adversaries deploy RMMs in layers: one documented case shows JumpCloud installing GetScreen, ScreenConnect, and SuperOps on the same host simultaneously, creating redundant footholds that survive single-agent removal (T1219) - ScreenConnect is nearly always a second-stage payload; its C2 domain often appears directly in the ScreenConnect.Client.exe command line, making process logs one of the few places a "malicious" domain is extractable without network inspection - NetSupport hides in C:\Users\Public\ or randomized folders; cracked copies use nonsense license strings like HANEYMANEY; network detection is reliable via User-Agent NetSupport Manager/1.3 - ITarian dropped DeerStealer and HijackLoader via sideloaded DLLs after staging through DicomPortable.exe; PDQ Connect stores its API token at C:\ProgramData\PDQ\PDQConnectAgent\token, which is the config artifact to pull in an investigation - MSIExec breaks the process tree: follow-on malicious activity runs under SYSTEM, severing the visible link to the phishing lure
Hunt for RMM binaries in Downloads or Public folders whose metadata names a known RMM product but whose filename says Invoice.exe or Statement.msi. If you find one RMM, hunt for two more. Baseline authorized tools against lolrmm[.]io.

item.title: FortiBleed — 75k Fortinet firewalls have admin passwords cracked
item.description:
75,000 Fortinet 🌐 firewall configs leaked with plaintext admin credentials, roughly 50% of all internet-facing FortiGate devices. Most are still online, most on recent patches, and the origin of the breach is unknown.
Key details: - Data confirmed legitimate by Hudson Rock. Includes full config exports with credentials visible only from the device itself. IP overlap with the 2025 Belsen Group leak (15k devices) is minimal, making this a largely separate, more recent compromise. - Fortinet moved to PBKDF2 credential storage in early-2025 firmware, but only re-hashes passwords after an admin logs in post-update. Devices patched but never re-authenticated still stored credentials as SHA-256 with salt, crackable offline. - The dataset is formatted with company name, revenue, and country, a standard eCrime initial-access broker format, suggesting this may be circulating for sale or already sold before publication. - In a majority of sampled devices the FortiGate management interface is exposed directly to the internet, giving any buyer of this data a direct login path to the firewall and the network behind it.
Takeaway: Rotate admin credentials on all FortiGate devices now, then force admins to log back in so PBKDF2 re-hashing triggers. Pull admin login logs and hunt for successful authentications you did not initiate. If you see unauthorized success events, treat the device as backdoored and replace it. Check hudsonrock[.]com/fortinet against your domains.

item.title: The Compromise of 30,000 Fortinet Firewalls
item.description:
Russian-speaking 🇷🇺 operators have built a self-feeding credential database of 30,791 verified working logins across Fortinet firewalls and VPN gateways in 194 countries, targeting banks, telecoms, hospitals, and government agencies with no zero-day required.
Key findings: - No vulnerability exploited. Attackers ran automated credential-stuffing using previously leaked Fortinet passwords, then passively sniffed traffic on compromised devices to harvest fresh credentials fed back into the scanner, a self-sustaining loop (T1110.004, T1557) - Default and generic accounts dominate: "admi*" alone covers 21% of entries. Built-in Fortinet system accounts make up the bulk of the rest, confirming mass failure to rename defaults or rotate factory credentials - Telecom is the hardest-hit sector (5,616 entries); government accounts for 591 entries across 111 domains, with Ukraine 🇺🇦, Poland 🇵🇱, and Taiwan heavily represented alongside NATO members, consistent with the geopolitical targeting pattern - The dataset has not appeared on criminal forums as of publication. Credentials are verified working. If your org is in it, treat access as confirmed, not theoretical
Responder action: pull FortiGate admin and SSL-VPN auth logs immediately and look for logins outside business hours or from unfamiliar source IPs. Rotate every credential, enforce MFA on all remote-access accounts, and block management interfaces from the public internet.

item.title: Malware à la Mode: Tracking Dropping Elephant Tradecraft Through a China-Themed Loader Chain
item.description:
Dropping Elephant resurfaces with a China-lure LNK chain delivering a fully in-memory RAT via DLL side-loading and Donut shellcode, with AMSI, WLDP, and ETW patched before execution.
Key findings: - Full chain: GRES3001.lnk (SHA256: a8ecbd9c...) spawns conhost.exe into obfuscated PowerShell, pulls payloads from chinagreenenergy[.]org, stages Fondue.exe, malicious APPWIZ.cpl (914da75a...), and encrypted editor.dat under C:\Users\Public\ and C:\Windows\Tasks\, then creates scheduled task "GoogleErrorReport" running Fondue.exe every minute (T1053.005, T1574.002) - APPWIZ.cpl decrypts editor.dat with AES-256-CBC, allocates RWX memory, and passes execution to Donut via EnumUILanguagesW callback proxy. Donut patches in-process AMSI, WLDP, and ETW, then maps the final 32-bit RAT (7099c339...) entirely in memory, nothing hits disk (T1620, T1562.001) - The in-memory RAT uses Salsa20-encrypted C2 fields (key: tn9905083tfbsxqrxs7qe4ryw1nif8h1), beacons to gcl-power[.]org:443 at /prjozifvkpkfhkr/gedhagammgjvvva/, and exfiltrates screenshots to a dedicated URI. Idle sentinel is MMMMM==YYYYY - Attribution rests on code-level overlaps with known Dropping Elephant samples: shared BitBlt screenshot logic, 0x2710 buffer constant, WININET request flow, and cmd.exe /c chcp 65001 shell pattern
Hunt for Fondue.exe loading APPWIZ.cpl outside System32, scheduled tasks with one-minute intervals pointing to C:\Users\Public\, and RWX memory regions in processes with patched AMSI stubs.

item.title: FishMonger’s arsenal upgraded: SprySOCKS for Windows
item.description:
FishMonger's 🇨🇳 SprySOCKS backdoor goes Windows: two undocumented variants (WIN_DRV and WIN_PLUS) add kernel-level rootkit stealth, TCP traffic diversion, and UEFI bootkit indicators to a previously Linux-only implant targeting government orgs in Honduras, Taiwan 🇹🇼, Thailand, and Pakistan 🇵🇰.
- Execution chain (WIN_DRV): batch script klelam00007.bat drops files to %SystemRoot%\Fonts\, creates scheduled task "ApphostRagistreationVerifier" (note the misspelling), and uses DLL side-loading via MFC satellite DLL (tpsvcloc.dll) to launch. Loader uses 128-bit AES-ECB (key: uXQLESMXGaRMs6BL) to decrypt payloads, then injects backdoor into svchost.exe via process doppelgänging (T1055.013), spawning from a spoolsv.exe token. TH-prefixed temp files in %TEMP% are a hunt artifact.
- RawWNPF kernel rootkit (WIN_DRV only): loaded in-memory via DriverLoader (fsdiskbit.sys, signed with leaked cert from PastDSE project), it hooks NtQuerySystemInformation to hide processes, hooks nsiproxy.sys IoCompletionRoutine to hide connections from netstat, registers WFP filters (named "Delivery Optimization" to blend in) to divert specially crafted TCP packets to the hidden backdoor port, and uses minifilter callbacks to hide files under \SystemRoot\Fonts\.
- WIN_PLUS persistence uses a malicious print processor: VSPMsg.dll at C:\Windows\System32\spool\prtprocs\x64\, registered under HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Print\Environments\Windows x64\Print Processors\VSPMsg.

item.title: The Intelligent Shield. OpenCTI
item.description:

- AI connector (INTERNAL_ENRICHMENT type) subscribes to RabbitMQ amq.topic exchange via pycti helper.listen(). On each Report, Malware, or Intrusion-Set create event, it calls Claude API with structured prompts and writes back: STIX Note (executive summary), threat actor/malware/AttackPattern relationships, x_opencti_score update. Content is truncated to 8000 chars per API call. Estimated cost: $0.01-$0.05 per report.
- Free feed connectors included: MITRE ATT&CK (confidence 90, TLP:WHITE), AlienVault OTX (confidence 60, TLP:GREEN), Abuse.ch URLhaus, MalwareBazaar, ThreatFox, Shodan InternetDB, NVD/CVE. Commercial connectors documented: Recorded Future, CrowdStrike, Mandiant, Intel 471.

item.title: No Patch Coming: The Arista EOS Tunnel Bug Your Scanner Will Miss
item.description:

Switch decapsulates and delivers without firewall traversal or host compromise - Detection gap: Arista published the advisory and CVE on May 5, 2026, flagging active exploitation. CVE did not propagate to public feeds for roughly a month. CISA KEV entry did not appear until June 9, creating a 5-week blind spot for automated workflows - Scanner failure: Version-based scanners are unreliable here as nearly all EOS versions are listed as affected. The vulnerable condition is a configured decap IP reachable from untrusted networks WITHOUT restricting ACLs, not a version string - A public PoC (fevvar54) exists. Treat exploitation as live and ongoing

item.title: Holding blobs for ransom: Four methods for Azure Storage ransomware
item.description:
Datadog Security Labs maps four distinct Azure Blob Storage ransomware vectors with full event codes and detection guidance. Two methods are confirmed in-the-wild; two are novel and undetected by current logging.
Key technical breakdown:
• Method 1 — Client-side encryption (BlackCat/Sphynx, observed): Attacker bulk downloads blobs, encrypts externally, reuploads. Requires only storage data-plane access (a leaked SAS token or access key is sufficient). Log artifacts: GetBlob + PutBlob only.
• Method 2 — Customer-Provided Keys (CPK, novel): Blobs reuploaded with AES-256 key material in `x-ms-encryption-key` HTTP header. Critical blind spot: Azure does NOT log the `x-ms-encryption-key-sha256` header — CPK PutBlob is IDENTICAL in logs to a normal PutBlob. Data-plane only. AWS deprecated SSE-C in Nov 2025; Azure still fully supports it.
• Method 3 — Encryption Scopes (STORM-0501, observed): Attacker creates Key Vault + encryption scope, re-encrypts all blobs, deletes the key. Logged: `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/encryptionScopes/write`, `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write`, `KeyCreate`, `KeyDelete`. Scope usage in PutBlob is NOT logged.
• Method 4 — Service Encryption CMK via cross-tenant Key Vault (novel): Single PATCH call to ARM API rotates the storage account's CMK to an attacker-controlled Key Vault in a foreign Entra tenant. No blob-level data-plane ops needed. Soft-delete protections are rendered useless as the key resides in attacker infrastructure.

item.description:

item.title: Factoring "short-sleeve" RSA keys with polynomials
item.description:
Trail of Bits discovers "short-sleeve" RSA keys with biased bit patterns can be factored using polynomial techniques. CompleteFTP bug (2016-2023) generated 603 vulnerable RSA keys and 74 DSA keys found in internet scans.
Key technical details: • CVE not assigned - Type mismatch in CompleteFTP genRandomBits() function copied 8-bit RNG output to 32-bit limbs, creating structured zero patterns • Affected CompleteFTP v10.0.0-12.0.0 (RSA) and v10.0.0-23.0.4 (DSA) with regularly spaced blocks of zero bits • Polynomial factorization converts modulus n to polynomial f_n(x) with small coefficients, exploiting limb structure • Pattern 1 (unexplained) found in expired certificates from Yahoo, Verizon; Pattern 2 traced to CompleteFTP SSH hosts
Attack methodology: • Researchers used base-2^w representation to find polynomials with exceptionally small coefficients from biased moduli • Factoring polynomials much easier than integer factorization - converts hard problem to easy one • Private key recovery possible when both prime factors exhibit short-sleeve property with structured zero patterns
DFIR artifacts and detection: • SSH banners identify CompleteFTP hosts running vulnerable versions • Certificate Transparency logs contain expired certificates with Pattern 1 bias • badkeys.info project now detects short-sleeve RSA keys automatically • Historical SSH scan data shows vulnerability spread from Dec 2016, plateaued after March 2019 fix

item.title: Below the OS, UEFI bootkits, firmware implants, and the artifacts Volatility will never find
item.description:
New deep-dive analysis reveals how UEFI bootkits and firmware implants operate below traditional DFIR tools, surviving disk replacement and OS reinstallation through persistence in motherboard flash memory and EFI System Partitions.
Key technical details: • BlackLotus bypasses Secure Boot via CVE-2022-21894, drops artifacts in \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\system32\ (illegitimate path) • CosmicStrand 🇨🇳 and MosaicRegressor persist in SPI flash, hooking CSMCORE DXE drivers before Windows loads • MoonBounce targets CORE_DXE firmware components, injecting shellcode into kernel memory with zero disk artifacts • FinSpy commercial spyware includes pre-OS bootkit component, proving technique moved beyond nation-state use
Detection methodology: • CHIPSEC for SPI flash analysis: `python chipsec_main.py -m common.bios_wp` checks write protection status • ESP imaging must be explicit - standard "full disk" acquisition may skip FAT32 EFI partition • TPM PCR baseline comparison detects boot chain tampering (PCR 0, 4, 7 are critical) • Secure Boot DBX currency validation - outdated revocation lists enable signed-but-vulnerable bootloader exploitation
Forensic limitations: • Volatility and memory forensics are structurally blind to firmware-layer persistence • Requires pre-incident firmware baselines and PCR values for meaningful analysis • False positives common without exact hardware revision and firmware version context

item.title: Header Manipulation: Bypasses, Probing, and the Security Audit Nobody Does
item.description:
New research reveals systematic header manipulation techniques for bypassing web application security controls. Comprehensive breakdown of Host header attacks, IP spoofing vectors, and 403 bypass patterns commonly exploited in penetration testing.
Key attack vectors: • Host header manipulation probes virtual hosts: `admin.target.com`, `internal.target.com`, `dev.target.com` revealing hidden interfaces • IP restriction bypass via X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Client-IP headers spoofing localhost (127.0.0.1) for admin panel access • Path normalization bypasses: trailing slashes (/admin/), URL encoding (%2fadmin), case variations (ADMIN) evading access controls • HTTP method switching from blocked GET to allowed POST/PUT/HEAD methods • CORS misconfiguration testing with reflected origins enabling credential theft
DFIR artifacts: • Web server access logs show suspicious header patterns: multiple X-Forwarded-For values, unusual Host headers, method anomalies • Application logs may reveal 403→200 status code transitions indicating successful bypasses • Network traffic analysis captures reflected CORS origins and security header absence
Detection opportunities: • Monitor for localhost/internal IP spoofing in proxy headers from external sources • Alert on Host header values not matching server's legitimate virtual hosts • Track unusual HTTP method usage on restricted endpoints

item.title: Marking Your Own Homework (Check Point Remote Access VPN IKEv1 Authentication Bypass CVE-2026-50751)
item.description:
Check Point hotfixes critical IKEv1 authentication bypass CVE-2026-50751 (CVSS 9.3) after month-long exploitation by Qilin ransomware affiliates. Logic flaw lets clients dictate their own certificate validation requirements.
Key technical details: • Affects R80.20.X through R82.10 Remote Access VPN/Mobile Access with IKEv1 enabled • VPNExtFeatures vendor ID payload (magic: 3cf187b24740...) writes client-controlled flags to auth gate at state+0x4bc4 • Setting bit 0x4 in trailing bytes bypasses verify_peer_auth() signature verification entirely • Exploitable over both UDP 500/4500 and TCP 443 "Visitor Mode" with identical technique • Works with self-signed certificates - only requires valid username and ICA organization string from gateway's public cert
Attack methodology: • Phase 1: Send VPNExtFeatures VID with 0x00000004 flag to disable signature checks • Phase 2: Present self-signed cert with valid DN (CN=username,OU=users,O=org) • Phase 3: Submit random signature payload - gateway accepts without verification • Result: Full phase-1 SA establishment and internal network access
DFIR artifacts: Look for IKE negotiations with "vendorid=0 .. not a Check Point peer" followed by successful "IkeSAFromState: User ... saved" entries. Monitor for certificate auth without corresponding valid trust chains.
